rows.subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
rows.description: A toddler in a home speaking Hindi, a mother tongue and English mixes words from all of them. This is normal and healthy; the child is sorting sounds and will separate them with time.

rows.subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
rows.description: A teenager mixes Hindi and English in every sentence with friends, and finds it natural and playful. Hinglish signals belonging to a generation, though switching to a cleaner register matters at exams and interviews.

rows.subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
rows.description: A young adult feels strong love for their state's language and bristles at Hindi or English being imposed. Pride is healthy; contempt for another language is not, and friendships cross these lines easily.
A young infant or toddler gives a broad open-mouth smile to a familiar face, showing pleasure and connection. Responding with a smile back builds the early conversation of attention.
A school-age child gives a small closed-mouth smile when meeting new people, often carrying shyness or politeness rather than delight. Giving time and not forcing a bigger smile respects temperament.
An angry child kicks and screams, needing help to calm before any talk can happen. A calm adult who stays nearby and names the feeling later teaches regulation.
A child hearing a parent shout freezes, shrinks or argues. Fear blocks understanding, and a later calm conversation is when the lesson can actually land.

A young child narrates events with imagination and exaggeration, blending fantasy with fact. It is developmentally normal, so adults gently separate pretend from real when facts matter, without harsh labels.
A teenager who reports something to an adult may be seeking safety or seeking revenge. Adults thank the teen, listen without assuming motives and act on safety concerns.
A young adult telling personal stories decides how much to share with whom. Sharing builds closeness, but oversharing with strangers or online may cause regret, so context and consent matter.
A toddler shows a bruise, says "scared" or points out something that happened. Early disclosure is brief and concrete; adults who respond calmly encourage later confiding.
A teenager tells a parent, teacher or counsellor about stress, mistakes or unsafe situations. Adults who listen first, stay calm and avoid instant punishment make later disclosure more likely.

rows.subtype: Admitting limits and needing help at work [Expressing]
rows.description: A young professional admits a gap, a mistake or a struggle to a manager or peer. Framed with a plan, it tends to build trust; risk depends on workplace culture, so choosing the listener matters.

A toddler rubs eyes, tugs at ears or presses the face into a parent when sleepy, hungry or unwell. The cue is ambiguous, so a caregiver checks the whole picture, such as feeding time, fever or noise, rather than one sign.

A schoolchild twirls hair, tugs a sleeve or straightens a uniform when nervous or self-conscious. These are common self-comfort acts, and observers should not read them as lying or flirting; they only show mild tension.

rows.subtype: Rubbing temples and neck at work [Expressing]
rows.description: A young professional rubs the neck or temples during long meetings, signalling tiredness, tension or headache. Colleagues cannot tell which from the gesture alone; offering a break or asking kindly is better than guessing.
